How to draw eyes

Eyes are the window to the soul, but drawing them isn't so easy. Here is how I draw eyes.

There are a few steps to drawing eyes:

  • Step 1: Draw a Circle

    • Our eyes are like spheres or balls. They are round but also not completely round. Start by drawing a circle so you have an Idea of the eyeball. It doesn't have to be perfect like in the image.


  • Step 2: Draw the upper lid of the eyes.

    • Now, if your drawing application has layers, make a new layer above the circle and reduce the opacity of the circle layer (I usually reduce it to 50%). The application I'll be using for this is Krita. If you are drawing on paper, just use an eraser to reduce the darkness of the circle. There are many different eye shapes: Upturned, Downturned, Almond, Monolid, Hooded, and Round. These are the main shapes. Upturned eyes are cat-like in their appearance and make a person seem sly. Downturned and round give an innocent or kind look. Almond eyes look like, well, Almonds. Monolids are quite similar to almond eyes. Last but not least, Hooded eyes give a look of maturity. The eye-shape I'll be drawing is my own eye-shape, Round.


  • Step 3: On the same layer, add the iris and pupil.

    • Now, where you are going to put the iris and pupil is up to you. I like to make the iris take up most of the eye, but not too much. Sometimes I make the pupil big, sometimes I don't. It just depends on my mood, lol. But here's a suggestion: the more evil the character, the smaller the pupil. Smaller pupils just give off that evil, crazy maniac look.


  • Step 4: Add the lower lid.

    • The placement of the lower lid is also up to you. If the lower lid overlaps with the iris, I suggest you erase some of the iris. If you want, you can play around with the liquify tool (if your application has it) to make the eye look like the shape you're going for. I made the eye a bit more round.


  • Step 5: Add the double eyelid.

    • This step is optional. You don't need to add the double-eyelid, especially if you're doing a monolid. How high or low you want it to be is up to you. You can also turn off the circle below. You don't need it anymore.


  • Step 6: Add the skin!

    • Now it's time to colour it in. Make a layer below and add any colour you want! Then you will set the lineart drawing (The eye) to the belending mode soft light or overlay (I prefer Soft Light). This only works if your drawing application has blending modes. If not, you'll have to colour the lineart manually by setting the layer to alpha lock, or you can make a clipping mask above.


  • Step 7: Block in the base colours.

    • Now, you will add the eye-white and iris. Make a layer about the skin. Here's a tip: never use pure white for the eye-white; despite the name, they usually aren't pure white. You can use a light grey or a lighter version of the skin colour. The iris colour is up to you. You don't have to colour it perfectly since you will (If you want) colour over them.


  • Step 8: Add the shadows around the eye.

    • Before we can get into rendering the eye, let's render around the eyes first. On a layer below, add shadows around the eye. To get my shadow colour, instead of just making the colour darker, I like to saturate the colour, darken it, and then move it a bit towards red on the colour wheel. I played around with the saturation, darkness and how red it is. For lighter colours on the face, I do the opposite. Afterwards, blend out most of the shadows and highlights. I suggest not blending out everything so that there can be contrast. In real life, the shadows we see, whether on an object or person, aren't all blended out. But you can blend everything or nothing at all if you want.


  • Step 9: Shade the Iris.

    • It's time to shade the eye! Woohoo! I like to start with the iris first. Remember, the eyeball is a sphere, so you have to shade it like one. You should shade the iris like you would a bowl. There's this part of the eye called the cornea.

    Now, because of it, when shading the iris, you'd shade it like a bowl. Now, I'm not going into the details because that's boring. Let me give you two examples. If the light is coming from above, the bottom of the eye would be lighter. If the light was coming from below, the top would be lighter! So, after figuring out where the light is coming from, I add the shading. I kept it simple. Then, I colour in the pupil using black. Now, this is a stylistic choice, but I like to lower the opacity of the brush and add some black to the top of the iris.


  • Step 10: Shade the eye-white.

    • It's time for the eye-white. There's nothing much to say; just know where the light is coming from and shade it like a sphere.


  • Step 11: Merge all layers

    • Everything's coming together, huh? Now it's time to merge all layers together for ...THE FINAL DETAILS! You will be shading on one layer for now.


  • Step 12: Add finishing touches.

    • Now you can go wild! But not too wild. Add more colours to the eye, define the upper lid, draw over some things, and add the eyelashes. If you want, you can add the lacrimal caruncle (the pink part of an eye). I also like to soften up the iris. Unfortunately for me, the computer did not record my drawing process; instead, it put the coding app I used the whole time instead of showing me adding details to the drawing. I apologize for this. Here's an image instead.


  • Step 13: Add the highlights.

    • Now, it is time to add the highlights. Make a new layer and set it to Add. My drawing application doesn't have the blending mode Add, so I have to use the blending mode Screen. Then, place the highlight depending on the lighting. You may add sparkles like I did, just for fun.


  • Step 14: Get a reference.

    • This isn't really a step, but I'd advise you to get reference images of eyes and study them. Thank you so much for reading (plus watching the videos), and God bless.
